newsitem.title: USA: U.S. calls for Afghan reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. calls for Afghan reconciliation.

text.p: The United States said on Friday it hopes the Taleban militia who took over Kabul will move toward national reconciliation and held out the possibility of establishing full diplomatic ties.

Noting an announcement by Taleban leaders that Afghans can return to Kabul without fear and the country is the common home of all Afghans, State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies said: "We take those statements as an indication that the Taleban intends to respect the rights of all Afghans."

"So our hope, at this stage, is that the new authorities in Kabul will move quickly to restore order and security and to form a representative interim government that can begin the process of reconciliation nationwide," he said.
The Taleban militia appealed on Friday for international recognition of its government after its forces captured the capital Kabul.

Two years after their formation, the one-time band of Islamic student vigilantes took over a ruined capital, hanged former president Najibullah and his brother and proclaimed the complete enforcement of Islam in the war-wracked country.
Despite the fact that the group had taken power by force, and hanged Najibullah, Davies said Washington had not ruled out recognising the new regime and establishing diplomatic relations.
"I just think it's really too early to pronounce ourselves on questions like diplomatic relations yet," he said.
Also, asked about the Taleban's intentions to impose Islamic law, Davies said: "At this stage, we're not reading anything into that."

He added that since the Taleban "appear to hold a majority of the cards at this stage, our call on them is to use their new position of authority to move to establish democratic institutions and to move to a process of national reconciliation."
"The extrajudicial action taken against Najibullah and his associates was a regrettable development," the spokesman said.
The United States has not had an embassy in Kabul since the Soviets left in the late 1980s. But there have been some low-level contacts with the Taleban, Davies said.
The spokesman said that Americans in Kabul who wanted to leave the capital as the Taleban approached have been evacuated but some Americans who made the choice to stay remain there.
